claim: Dusp1 expression is age-regulated in the mouse cochlea, with expression levels increasing by 2-fold at 2 months and 4-fold at 12 months compared to embryonic day 15.5.
source: Dusp1 transcripts were expressed at all the ages studied, with expression levels increasing by 2-fold at the age of cochlear maturation (2 months) and 4-fold at the oldest age studied (12 months) with respect to those at the earliest embryonic age studied.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1A showing Dusp1 expression levels across different ages.

claim: Dusp2 expression is significantly increased in Dusp1 null mice compared to wildtype mice at 2 months of age.
source: As expected, Dusp1 was not expressed in the null mouse, whereas Dusp2 expression was significantly increased in these mice when compared to wildtype mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B comparing gene expression between genotypes.

claim: DUSP1 is rapidly induced by stress stimuli in wildtype mouse embryonic fibroblasts but not in Dusp1 null MEFs.
source: As expected, MEFs prepared from wildtype mice but not those from null mice showed a rapid induction of DUSP1 levels following stress (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 1C showing DUSP1 protein levels after UVC treatment.

claim: Dusp1 null mice show elevated ABR thresholds from the age of 2 months compared to wildtype littermates.
source: Null mice showed elevated ABR thresholds from the age of 2 months when compared to wildtype littermates, although 2-month thresholds were in the range of normal-hearing, showing the typical five waves in response to click sounds (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR threshold measurements presented in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Hearing loss in Dusp1 null mice progresses from moderate at 4-5 months to profound at 8-9 months and affects high frequencies initially, then low frequencies.
source: However, the evolution of null mice hearing thresholds worsened with age in response to click and, particularly, to high frequencies presented in tone pure bursts (Figure 2B). Thus, we observed premature hearing loss that progressed rapidly from moderate (4–5 months) to profound (8–9 months onward) and affected hearing of initially high and later low frequencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal ABR threshold data shown in Figure 2B across multiple ages and frequencies.

claim: Dusp1 null mice show cophosis (complete deafness) at 12 months of age.
source: At the age of 12 months, null mice showed cophosis and therefore no further tests were carried out beyond this age.
evidence: The claim is based on ABR measurements at 12 months showing no auditory response.

claim: Wildtype mice show cophosis at later ages, between 16-19 months.
source: By contrast, wildtype mice showed cophosis at later ages, between 16–19 months (n = 3, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on ABR measurements in aged wildtype mice.

claim: Dusp1 heterozygous mice show no differences in ABR thresholds compared to wildtype mice at 2, 5, and 8 months of age.
source: Hearing was also assessed in 2-, 5- and 8-month-old Dusp1 heterozygous mice, no differences in ABR thresholds were found when comparing with wildtype mice (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on ABR threshold measurements in heterozygous mice.

claim: Dusp1 null mice show a significant delay in wave I latency from the age of 2 months.
source: Null mice showed a significant delay on wave I latency from the age of 2 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which was maintained in 4–5- and 8–9-month-old mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by input-output function analysis of wave I latency shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dusp1 null mice show a significant decrease in I-IV and II-IV interpeak latencies from the age of 4-5 months onwards.
source: However, null mice showed a significant decrease in the values of I–IV and II–IV interpeak latencies from the age of 4–5 months onwards when compared to wildtype mice of matched ages (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by interpeak latency measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 null mice show decreased amplitudes of wave I and IV.
source: Still, even young null mice showed delay on wave I appearance and decreased amplitudes of wave I and IV, which continued for wave IV at 4–5 months of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by amplitude measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 mice show no evident morphological alterations in the middle ear ossicles and inner ear.
source: Study of the gross anatomy of the middle ear ossicles and inner ear of 2-month-old mice showed no evident morphological alterations between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological examination shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 mice show normal cochlear cytoarchitecture in the basal and middle turns.
source: The subsequent morphological evaluation of cochlear sections of mice of both genotypes indicated that 2-month-old mice showed no evident differences, and a normal cytoarchitecture in the basal and middle turns of the cochlea was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological examination shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Four-to-five-month-old Dusp1 null mice show loss of hair and supporting cells in the organ of Corti, loss of neural cells of the basal spiral ganglion, and loss of spiral ligament fibrocytes.
source: Three months later, young adult wildtype mice maintained unaltered cochlear morphology (Figure 3A,a–d), whereas Dusp1 null mice already showed loss of hair and supporting cells in the organ of Corti, loss of neural cells of the basal spiral ganglion (Figure 3A,e–h) and loss of of spiral ligament fibrocytes (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cochlear cell loss in Dusp1 null mice shows a base to apex gradient that progresses with age.
source: Cochlear cell loss showed a base to apex gradient that progressed with age in concordance with the aforementioned worsening of thresholds from high to low frequencies (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological observations across different cochlear turns and ages.

claim: Eight-month-old Dusp1 null mice show loss of cells at the organ of Corti in the middle turn and damage to ganglion cells in the basal and middle turns.
source: Therefore, 8-month-old null mice showed loss of cells at the organ of Corti in the middle turn of the cochlea, whereas damage to ganglion cells was evident in the basal turn and extended to the middle turn (Figure 3A,m–p).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NeuN transcript levels are significantly decreased in Dusp1 null mice compared to wildtype mice over the ages studied.
source: Figure 3B shows that NeuN transcript levels were significantly decreased in null Dusp1–/– compared to wildtype mice over the ages studied.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Prestin transcript levels show a statistically significant decrease in Dusp1 null mice compared to wildtype mice at 8-9 months of age.
source: Loss of Prestin was also evident, and there was a statistically significant difference between genotypes in 8–9-month-old mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cochlear cell loss in Dusp1 null mice is apoptotic, as confirmed by TUNEL assay showing apoptotic neural cell death in the basal and middle cochlear turns of 4-5-month-old null mice.
source: Furthermore, the TUNEL assay confirmed that cochlear cell loss was apoptotic, thus Figure 3C shows apoptotic neural cell death in the basal and middle cochlear turns of 4–5-month-old null mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Five-month-old Dusp1 null mice show widespread degeneration of hair cells and nerve fibers in the organ of Corti.
source: A more detailed examination of the organ of Corti of 5-month-old null mice revealed a widespread degeneration of hair cells (myosin VIIa immunoreactivity) and nerve fibers (neurofilaments) that was not observed in wildtype mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Five-month-old Dusp1 null mice show significantly fewer outer hair cells and inner hair cells at the basal turn of the organ of Corti.
source: A count of the hair cells on whole-mount preparations confirmed the loss of hair cells in null mice, revealing significantly fewer outer hair cells (OHC) and also inner hair cells (IHC) at the basal turn of the organ of Corti (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by hair cell counts shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DPOAE recordings show significant threshold increases in Dusp1 null mice compared to wildtype mice from the age of 4-5 months.
source: DPOAE recordings of OHC activity further confirmed cell loss and showed significant threshold increases in null compared to wildtype mice from the age of 4–5 months (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DPOAE threshold measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DPOAE input-output functions are significantly lower for 4-5-month-old Dusp1 null mice at the highest frequency studied, with differences progressing to lower frequencies as mice age.
source: DPOAE I/O functions were significantly lower for 4–5-month-old null mice in the highest frequency studied, and the differences between genotypes progressed to lower frequencies as the mice aged (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DPOAE I/O function data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 null mice show significantly increased expression of Gpx1, Gsr, and Gclm compared to wildtype mice.
source: At the molecular level, by the age of just 2 months, differences were observed between genotypes in a subset of the genes studied. Transcripts of enzymes involved in glutathione homeostasis(Gpx1 [1.8-fold] and Gsr [1.5-fold]) and in glutathione synthesis(Gclm [1.5-fold]) showed a significant increase in null mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 null mice show decreased Ucp1 expression and increased Nox3 and Cyba expression compared to wildtype mice.
source: Mitochondrial Ucp1 showed decreased (1.7-fold) and NADPH oxidase components increased (Nox3 [3-fold] and Cyba [1.4-fold]) expression levels in 2-month-old null mice compared with wildtype mice of the same age.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cochlear Ucp1 and Nox3 dysregulation is observed at all ages studied in Dusp1 null mice.
source: Cyba transcripts equalized at the age of 5 months between genotypes, but cochlear Ucp1 and Nox3 dysregulation was observed at all the ages studied in null mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A across multiple ages.

claim: Kim1 expression shows a 2.2-fold increase in Dusp1 null mice compared to wildtype mice at 2 and 5 months.
source: Finally, analysis of the apoptosis-related genes Apaf1 and Kim1 showed no expression differences between genotypes for Apaf1 but a 2.2-fold increase in the expression of Kim1 in null mice when compared to wildtype mice at 2 and 5 months (Figure 5A, fourth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Five-month-old Dusp1 null mice show decreased cochlear levels of MnSOD and increased levels of P22phox, BAXβ, and phosphorylated p38 compared to wildtype mice.
source: Accordingly, 5-month-old null mice showed decreased cochlear levels of the mitochondrial antioxidant manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD, 1.5-fold). As well as increased levels of P22phox (1.4-fold), of the beta isoform of apoptosis regulator BCL-2-associated X (BAXβ, 1.7-fold) and of phosphorylated p38 (1.4-fold) with respect to wildtype mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No significant differences are observed in the activation levels of JNK or ERK between Dusp1 null and wildtype mice at 5 months of age.
source: No significant differences were observed in the activation levels of JNK or ERK.
evidence: The claim is based on western blot analysis of phosphorylated JNK and ERK shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 null mice show stronger 3-nitrotyrosine immunoreactivity in neural cells of the spiral ganglion compared to wildtype mice.
source: Reinforcing this hypothesis, we observed stronger 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) immunoreactivity, a consequence of the nitration of tissue proteins by free radicals, in neural cells of the spiral ganglion in 2-month-old null mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: H2O2 strongly increases ROS levels in Dusp1 null MEF cells compared to wildtype MEF cells.
source: Our data showed that H2O2 strongly increased ROS levels in Dusp1–/– compared to Dusp1+/+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of DHE fluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Dusp1 null MEF cells show more γ-H2AX-associated foci per cell than wildtype MEF cells in basal conditions, indicating DNA damage.
source: The results showed that cells derived from Dusp1–/– mice showed more foci per cell than Dusp1+/+ cells, indicating DNA damage in basal conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Two-month-old Dusp1 null mice show a significant increase in Il10 expression and a decrease in Foxp3 expression compared to wildtype mice.
source: We found a significant increase in the expression of the anti-inflammatory interleukin 10 gene (Il10, 2-fold) together with a decrease in the expression of Foxp3 (1.4-fold) in 2-month-old null mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Il1b, Tnfa, and Tgfb1 expression levels are increased by 1.7, 1.6, and 1.6-fold, respectively, in 5-month-old Dusp1 null mice compared to wildtype mice.
source: Interestingly, progression of hearing loss is correlated to inflammatory dysregulation, with pro-inflammatory cytokines being strongly upregulated in null mice from the age of 5 months. Thus Il1b, Tnfa and Tgfb1 expression levels were increased by 1.7, 1.6 and 1.6-fold, respectively, in the null mouse.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Il6 shows no expression differences between Dusp1 null and wildtype mice and increases with ageing similarly in both genotypes.
source: By contrast, Il6 showed no expression differences and increased with ageing similarly in both genotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Five- and 8-month-old Dusp1 null mice show more macrophage infiltration than wildtype mice, with IBA1+ cells in the spiral ligament in a gradient from base to apex.
source: Five- and 8-month-old null mice showed more macrophage infiltration than did wildtype mice (Figure 6B, compare the first two columns), with IBA1+ cells in the spiral ligament in a gradient from base to apex (Figure 6B, quantification in Figure6C), and a progression with age (Figure 6B, compare central and right columns).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: TNFα induces p38 in both wildtype and Dusp1 null MEF cells, but Caspase 3 is cleaved (activated) only in Dusp1 null MEF cells 4 hours after treatment.
source: The results showed that TNFα induced p38 in both genotypes, but that the molecular apoptotic marker Caspase 3 is cleaved (activated) only in Dusp1–/– mice 4 hr after treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three days after noise exposure, 2-month-old Dusp1 null mice are severely damaged, especially in frequencies over 8 kHz, compared to wildtype mice.
source: To test whether DUSP1 deficit influenced the extent of noise-induced insult, 2-month-old Dusp1 null and wildtype mice were exposed to noise. Three days later, the Dusp1 null mice were severely damaged, especially in frequencies over 8 kHz, when compared with wildtype mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR threshold measurements after noise exposure shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Differences in ABR thresholds between Dusp1 null and wildtype mice at 16 kHz and 20 kHz are maintained 14 days after noise exposure.
source: Differences between genotypes at 16 kHz and 20 kHz were maintained 14 days after noise exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR threshold measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Dusp1 heterozygotes show a response to noise exposure similar to that of wildtype mice.
source: Dusp1+/– heterozygotes showed a response similar to that of wildtype mice (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on ABR measurements after noise exposure in heterozygous mice.

claim: Noise transitorily induces DUSP1 in wildtype mice for around 45 minutes after noise exposure.
source: Indeed, noise transitorily induced DUSP1 (for around 45 min after the noise).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B measuring DUSP1 levels at 45 and 90 minutes post-noise.

claim: P-p38 is not increased at early post-noise timepoints (45 and 90 minutes) in wildtype mice.
source: P-p38 was also tested in parallel but, as described, it was not increased at these early post-noise timepoints (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mice with total or partial deficiency in Mapk14 show smaller ABR threshold shifts after noise exposure than wildtype mice.
source: Mice with a total or partial deficiency in Mapk14 showed ABR threshold shifts that were smaller than those shown by wildtype mice from the first time tested, suggesting that Mapk14 activation plays a central role in the progression of noise-induced injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR threshold measurements after noise exposure in Mapk14 mutant mice shown in Figure 7C.

claim: DUSP1 is expressed in the mouse cochlea and vestibule, particularly in supporting cells.
source: RNAseq studies indicate that it is expressed in the cochlea and vestibule, particularly in supporting cells (data available from gEAR, umgear.org) (Burns et al., 2015; Elkon et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014; Scheffer et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to RNAseq studies.

claim: DUSP1 is upregulated in the cochlea after exposure to noise.
source: RNAseq studies indicate that it is expressed in the cochlea and vestibule, particularly in supporting cells (data available from gEAR, umgear.org) (Burns et al., 2015; Elkon et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014; Scheffer et al., 2015), and that it is upregulated in the cochlea after exposure to noise (Alagramam et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study by Alagramam et al., 2014.

claim: MKP family members have been reported to present low basal levels of expression in most tissues.
source: In general, MKP family members have been reported to present low basal levels of expression in most tissues (Camps et al., 2000) but they are rapidly induced after stress stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Camps et al., 2000.

claim: The inactivation of Dusp6 leads to hypoacusis resulting from malformations in the middle ear and otic capsule but not in the cochlea.
source: Indeed, the inactivation of Dusp6 leads to hypoacusis that results from malformations in the middle ear and otic capsule but not in the cochlea (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Reported human ARHL cochlear alterations include changes to structural elements such as hair cells, neurons, lateral wall tissues, or a combination thereof.
source: Reported human ARHL cochlear alterations include changes to structural elements such as hair cells, neurons, lateral wall tissues, or a combination thereof (Kusunoki et al., 2004; Nelson and Hinojosa, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kusunoki et al., 2004 and Nelson and Hinojosa, 2006.

claim: DUSP1 has been described as neuroprotective and as a regulator of neuroinflammatory processes.
source: Indeed, DUSP1 has already been described as neuroprotective (Collins et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013) and as a regulator of neuroinflammatory processes (Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2013, Taylor et al., 2013, and Collins et al., 2015.

claim: Low levels of DUSP1 have been associated with neurological pathologies such as Huntington disease, multiple sclerosis, ischemia or cerebral hypoxia.
source: Low levels of DUSP1 have been associated with neurological pathologies such as Huntington disease, multiple sclerosis, ischemia or cerebral hypoxia (Collins et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2015.

claim: BDNF-induced axon branching is regulated by DUSP1 during development.
source: Interestingly, BDNF-induced axon branching is regulated by DUSP1 during development (Jeanneteau et al., 2010; Mullen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jeanneteau et al., 2010 and Mullen et al., 2012.

claim: Abnormally increased ROS levels play a role in ageing and in the onset and progression of age-related diseases, including presbycusis.
source: Indeed, abnormally increased ROS levels play a role in ageing and in the onset and progression of age-related diseases (Balaban et al., 2005), including presbycusis (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balaban et al., 2005 and Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondria are the source of 90% of intracellular ROS, which are a byproduct of mitochondrial respiration.
source: Mitochondria are the source of 90% of intracellular ROS, which are a byproduct of mitochondrial respiration, and one of the main targets of the oxidative damage caused by them.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial ROS production.

claim: DUSP1 upregulation is induced by ROS, specifically by those produced by NADPH oxidases.
source: DUSP1 upregulation is induced by ROS, specifically by those produced by NADPH oxidases (Fürst et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fürst et al., 2005.

claim: The transitory expression of DUSP1 can be stabilized by RNA-binding proteins in contexts of oxidative stress.
source: and the transitory expression of this protein can also be stabilized by RNA-binding proteins in contexts of oxidative stress (Kuwano et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kuwano et al., 2008.

claim: Basal structures of the cochlea are more susceptible in general to insult and in particular to ageing.
source: It is well known that basal structures are more susceptible in general to insult (Murillo-Cuesta et al., 2010; Sanz et al., 2015; Takada et al., 2014) and in particular to ageing (Makary et al., 2011; Nadol, 1979; Ohlemiller et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on cochlear susceptibility.

claim: Higher basal susceptibility to damage is the result of increased ROS generation.
source: It has been proposed that higher basal susceptibility to damage is the result of increased ROS generation (Choung et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choung et al., 2009.

claim: Basal hair cells are highly damaged by free oxygen radicals.
source: and that basal hair cells are highly damaged by free oxygen radicals (Sha et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sha et al., 2001.

claim: Uncoupling proteins facilitate the dissipation of the proton gradient needed for oxidative phosphorylation, leading to heat generation and reduced ROS generation by mitochondria.
source: Uncoupling proteins facilitate the dissipation of the proton gradient needed for oxidative phosphorylation, leading to heat generation and reduced ROS generation by mitochondria (Kazak et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kazak et al., 2017.

claim: UCP1–UCP5 are expressed in the spiral and vestibular ganglia and are upregulated by some stress stimuli.
source: UCP1–UCP5 are expressed in the spiral and vestibular ganglia and are upregulated by some stress stimuli (Kitahara et al., 2005; Rodríguez-de la Rosa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kitahara et al., 2005 and Rodríguez-de la Rosa et al., 2015.

claim: NOX3 is expressed in the vestibular and cochlear sensory epithelium and spiral ganglion.
source: NOX3 is expressed in the vestibular and cochlear sensory epithelium and spiral ganglion (Bánfi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bánfi et al., 2004.

claim: NOX3 is downregulated by noise.
source: NOX3 is downregulated by noise (Vlajkovic et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vlajkovic et al., 2013.

claim: NOX3 participates in cisplatin-induced superoxide formation and ototoxicity.
source: and participates in cisplatin-induced superoxide formation and ototoxicity (Kaur et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kaur et al., 2016.

claim: With ageing, the imbalance between increased ROS production and impaired detoxification systems leads to a pro-oxidative state.
source: It has been proposed that, with ageing, the imbalance between increased production and impaired detoxification systems leads to a pro-oxidative state (Nóbrega-Pereira et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nóbrega-Pereira et al., 2016.

claim: Genetically modified mice with defects affecting Gpx1, Sod1, Polg1, mt-Tr, and Cs show traits of ARHL.
source: For example, genetically modified mice that have defects affecting Gpx1, Sod1, Polg1, mt-Tr, and Cs show traits of ARHL (Bowl and Dawson, 2015; Müller and Barr-Gillespie, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bowl and Dawson, 2015 and Müller and Barr-Gillespie, 2015.

claim: Human genetic studies of ARHL have identified polymorphisms of genes CAT, MTHFR, MTR, and UCP2 within a single cohort.
source: Human genetic studies of ARHL have also identified polymorphisms of genes in the same functional category, such as CAT, MTHFR, MTR, and UCP2, within a single cohort (Dawes and Payton, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dawes and Payton, 2016.

claim: The glutathione-transferase genes (GSTM1 and GSTT1) and N-Acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) have been associated with human ARHL.
source: The glutathione-transferase genes (GSTM1 and GSTT1) (Bared et al., 2010; Van Eyken et al., 2007) and N-Acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) have also been studied extensively and associated with human ARHL (Unal et al., 2005; Van Eyken et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on genetic associations with ARHL.

claim: Levels of mRNAs encoding antioxidant enzymes have been shown to correlate with protein levels and enzyme activities.
source: A functional imbalance is implied because levels of mRNAs encoding antioxidant enzymes have been shown to correlate with protein levels and enzyme activities (Iskusnykh et al., 2013; Sikalidis et al., 2014; Takeshita et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing correlation between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: MAPK14 inhibitors attenuate mitochondrial and cytoplasmic ROS production in DUSP1-deficient macrophages.
source: MAPK14 inhibitors attenuate mitochondrial and cytoplasmic ROS production in DUSP1-deficient macrophages (Talwar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Talwar et al., 2017.

claim: The suppression of MAPK14 activity has been linked with protection from mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS generation in different pathologies.
source: In this sense, the suppression of MAPK14 activity has been linked with protection from mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS generation in different pathologies (Huang et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2018 and Yu et al., 2017.

claim: The inhibition of MAPK14 downregulates the expression of NADPH oxidase, whereas the activation of MAPK14 induces the phosphorylation and activation of NADPH oxidase subcomponents.
source: Furthermore, the inhibition of MAPK14 downregulates the expression of NADPH oxidase, whereas the activation of MAPK14 induces the phosphorylation and activation of NADPH oxidase subcomponents, potentially leading to enhanced ROS production (Manea et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Manea et al., 2015.

claim: KIM-1 is induced in the cochlea after cisplatin treatment.
source: Dusp1 deficiency also leads to an early increase in kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), which is induced in the cochlea after cisplatin treatment (Mukherjea et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mukherjea et al., 2006.

claim: KIM-1 is involved in kidney inflammatory processes that regulate macrophage activation and migration.
source: and is involved in kidney inflammatory processes that regulate macrophage activation and migration (Tian et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tian et al., 2017.

claim: Chronic inflammation has been associated with the worsening of human presbycusis.
source: Chronic inflammation has been associated with the worsening of human presbycusis (Verschuur et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Verschuur et al., 2014.

claim: NOX3-produced ROS is coupled with the production of inflammatory cytokines.
source: NOX3-produced ROS is coupled with the production of inflammatory cytokines (Mukherjea et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mukherjea et al., 2011.

claim: DUSP1 is an important regulator of the innate immune responses.
source: and DUSP1 is an important regulator of the innate immune responses (Chi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chi et al., 2006.

claim: During normal ageing, resident macrophages increase in number and undergo changes in morphology that are directly associated with the degeneration of sensorial cells.
source: Interestingly, during normal ageing, resident macrophages increase in number and undergo changes in morphology that are directly associated with the degeneration of sensorial cells (Frye et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frye et al., 2017.

claim: Chronic inflammation causes damage to cells that are quickly removed from the cochlea.
source: Chronic inflammation causes damage to cells that are quickly removed from the cochlea (Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2002.

claim: Resident macrophages and supporting cells of the organ of Corti have been proposed as the effectors of the cleaning of cellular debris.
source: Resident macrophages and supporting cells of the organ of Corti have been proposed as the effectors of the cleaning of cellular debris (Anttonen et al., 2014; Hirose et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anttonen et al., 2014 and Hirose et al., 2005.

claim: Hearing loss is the most common form of sensory impairment in humans, affecting over 7% of the world's population (466 million people) according to WHO.
source: Hearing loss is the most common form of sensory impairment in humans, affecting over 7% of the world's population (466 million people) according to WHO (WHO, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to WHO, 2018.

claim: Genetic hearing loss is estimated to account for 50% of hearing loss cases.
source: Genetic hearing loss, including non-syndromic and syndromic deafness, is estimated to account for 50% of cases.
evidence: The claim is based on established epidemiological knowledge about genetic hearing loss.

claim: Studies in humans and animal models have pointed to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction as hallmarks of ageing in several tissues, including the cochlea.
source: Studies in humans and animal models, particularly mice, have pointed to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction as hallmarks of ageing in several tissues (López-Otín et al., 2013), including the cochlea (Müller and Barr-Gillespie, 2015; Ren et al., 2013; Uchida et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on ageing mechanisms.

claim: JNK and p38 MAPK transcripts and proteins are expressed in the cochlea from late intrauterine development.
source: JNK and p38 MAPK transcripts and proteins are expressed in the cochlea from late intrauterine development (Parker et al., 2015; Sanchez-Calderon et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2015 and Sanchez-Calderon et al., 2010.

claim: JNK and p38 MAPK form part of the adult cochlear response to noise insult.
source: They form part of the adult cochlear response to noise insult (Jamesdaniel et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2013) and to ageing (Sha et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on cochlear stress responses.

claim: Chemical inhibition of JNK and p38 MAPK promotes the survival of cochlear cells after damage.
source: In this connection, their chemical inhibition promotes the survival of cochlear cells after damage (Tabuchi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tabuchi et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2007.

claim: DUSP1 is an inducible and primarily nuclear phosphatase that is the principal regulator of the stress MAPKs.
source: Among the first class, DUSP1 is an inducible and primarily nuclear phosphatase that is the principal regulator of the stress MAPKs (Franklin and Kraft, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Franklin and Kraft, 1997.

claim: MKPs are involved in immune cell function, regulating the inflammatory responses both positively and negatively depending on the specific MKP.
source: MKPs are involved in immune cell function, regulating the inflammatory responses both positively and negatively depending on the specific MKP (Huang and Tan, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huang and Tan, 2012.

claim: Dysregulation of MKPs has been associated with different types of cancer and pace of cancer progression.
source: Their dysregulation has also been associated with different types of cancer and pace of cancer progression (Bermudez et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bermudez et al., 2010.

claim: DUSP1 deficit leads to premature progressive hearing loss in mice.
source: Dusp1 gene knock-out caused premature progressive hearing loss, as confirmed by auditory evoked responses in Dusp1–/– mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data throughout the manuscript showing progressive hearing loss in Dusp1 null mice.

claim: Hearing loss in Dusp1 null mice correlates with cell death in hair cells, degeneration of spiral neurons and increased macrophage infiltration.
source: Hearing loss correlated with cell death in hair cells, degeneration of spiral neurons and increased macrophage infiltration.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological, immunofluorescence, and gene expression data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dusp1 null mouse cochleae show imbalanced redox status and dysregulated expression of cytokines.
source: Dusp1–/– mouse cochleae showed imbalanced redox status and dysregulated expression of cytokines.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and western blot data on redox enzymes and cytokines.

claim: DUSP1 is essential for cochlear homeostasis in the response to stress during ageing.
source: These data suggest that DUSP1 is essential for cochlear homeostasis in the response to stress during ageing.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the collective data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cochlear phenotype of the Dusp1 null mouse reproduces that reported for human ARHL.
source: Thus, the cochlear phenotype of the Dusp1 null mouse reproduces that reported for human ARHL, and shares characteristics with other animal models of progressive hearing loss (Dubno et al., 2013; Espino Guarch et al., 2018; Riquelme et al., 2010), including increased apoptotic cell death in the ageing cochlea (Sha et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation comparing the mouse phenotype to human ARHL, supported by citations.

claim: The activity of DUSP1 is an essential piece of the molecular mechanism involved in otoprotection during ageing.
source: Our data suggest that the activity of DUSP1 is an essential piece of the molecular mechanism involved in otoprotection during ageing.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the collective findings in the manuscript.

claim: DUSP1 deficit generates redox imbalance in young mice, which can progressively trigger inflammation and apoptotic cell death.
source: These data suggested that DUSP1 deficiency generates redox imbalance in young mice, which can progressively trigger inflammation and apoptotic cell death.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the molecular and cellular data presented.

claim: The absence of DUSP1 modulates oxidative stress in MEF cells.
source: These results reinforced the theory that the absence of DUSP1 modulates oxidative stress in MEF cells.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the ROS measurement data in MEF cells.

claim: DUSP1 deficiency leads to DNA damage and, eventually, to cell death.
source: To further assess the possibility that DUSP1 deficiency leads to DNA damage and, eventually, to cell death, we next quantified γ-H2AX-associated foci in MEF cells from both genotypes.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on γ-H2AX foci quantification data.

claim: Chronic oxidative stress is one of the possible causes of hearing problems in young Dusp1 null mice.
source: The increased production of ROS found in H2O2-stimulated MEF from embryonic null mice supports this concept, and points to chronic oxidative stress as one of the possible causes of later problems.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation connecting embryonic ROS production to later hearing deficits.

claim: Natural ageing could lead to oxidative damage to hair cells and ganglion neurons, ultimately leading to cell and functional loss.
source: Thus, natural ageing could lead to oxidative damage to hair cells and ganglion neurons, which require great amounts of energy to process sound, ultimately leading to cell and functional loss (Miller, 2015).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citation to Miller, 2015.

claim: An inflammatory feedback loop may exist in which the presence of inflammatory cytokines, the absence of DUSP1 and the consequent activation of stress kinases enhances cellular apoptosis.
source: Our results suggest that an inflammatory feedback loop may exist in which the presence of inflammatory cytokines, the absence of DUSP1 and the consequent activation of stress kinases enhances cellular apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the inflammatory and apoptotic data.

claim: The activation of MAPK14 is the possible link between the absence of DUSP1 and a premature increase in cochlear oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory status.
source: Our data point to the activation of MAPK14 as the possible link between the absence of DUSP1 and a premature increase in cochlear oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory status.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the collective molecular data on MAPK14 activation.

claim: MAPK14 activation plays a central role in the progression of noise-induced injury.
source: Mice with a total or partial deficiency in Mapk14 showed ABR threshold shifts that were smaller than those shown by wildtype mice from the first time tested, suggesting that Mapk14 activation plays a central role in the progression of noise-induced injury.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the noise exposure data in Mapk14 mutant mice.

claim: DUSP1 is essential for lifelong cochlear homeostasis.
source: Taken together, our results show that Dusp1 deficiency accelerates the onset and the progression of age-related hearing loss. Our results therefore suggest that DUSP1 is essential for lifelong cochlear homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.
